meta.title: Sentiment analysis of political communication: combining a dictionary approach with crowdcoding

extraction.title: Sentiment analysis of political communication: combining a dictionary approach with crowdcoding
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (1027 lines, PDF pages 1-23): front matter, abstract, introduction, measurement section, crowdcoding and dictionary construction, validation, both applications, conclusions, Appendices 1-6 and the full reference list. Paul supplied no markup files (the "(none)" list is empty), so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or sticky notes were read. The paper has no content on lobbying, networks, path-finding, resource allocation, persuasion or turnout as analysis topics; it touches elections only through negative campaigning and media tone, and it touches legislators only through party press releases and parliamentary debates as corpus sources.
extraction.research_question: Can a negative sentiment dictionary for a language and domain of choice be built cheaply through crowdcoding, and does its word-based tonality score validly measure fine-grained negativity relative to expert and crowd coding? The authors illustrate use with (a) negative campaigning among Austrian parties in the 2013 national election and (b) media tonality toward parties and candidates.
extraction.theory: Sentiment as gradual negativity or tonality (not binary polarity), with a bag-of-words assumption and only the neutral-to-negative range covered because of negativity asymmetry (Peeters 1971; Baumeister et al. 2001; Rozin and Royzman 2001). Negativity bias in news (Galtung and Ruge 1965). Negative campaigning intensity matters for voters (Mutz and Reeves 2005; Fridkin and Kenney 2011). Government and coalition-partner restraint in attacks (Walter and Van der Brug 2013; Dolezal et al. 2015); electoral losers attack more (Damore 2002).
extraction.data: Unit of rating: sentences (coded by crowd coders); word-level scores are derived from sentences. Source corpus: about 470,000 sentences from Austrian party press releases, parliamentary debate minutes and media reports on election campaigns, 1995-2013 (Sec. 4.1). Seed-word prefilter reduced it to about 215,000 sentences; 13,000 were randomly drawn; 12,713 remained after removing duplicates and incomplete sentences (fn 5). Crowd sample: about 130,000 valid codings, 10 per sentence, from 480 coders on CrowdFlower (Austria/Germany only), cost about 2,000 EUR (about 2,200 USD; Table 7 sums to about 2,198 USD). Resulting dictionary: 5,001 unique word forms (Sec. 4.5). Validation sample: 200 sentences from party press releases of four national campaigns (2002-2013) plus media reports from the most recent campaign, coded by two expert authors and ten lay coders (Sec. 6). Extended validation: 755 negative party press release statements from the 2013 campaign, single expert coder (App. 3). Application 1: 1,958 party press releases from the final 6 weeks of the 2013 campaign, of which 755 are directed negative relations between two parties (612 with a tonality score per Table 2; 619 observations in Table 3). Application 2: 15,096 news reports from 15 Austrian dailies, final 8 weeks of the 2013 campaign, 439,954 sentences, about one in five referring to a party or top candidate.
extraction.method: Five-step procedure (Sec. 4): (1) sample sentences containing seed negative words; (2) crowdcode each sentence on a 0-4 negativity scale (0 not negative to 4 very strongly negative) plus an "uncodable" option, with test questions (4 initial, 1 in 5 later; two adjacent categories accepted); coders below 75% test accuracy excluded; (3) sentence score = mean of 10 coder ratings; (4) word score = mean of sentence scores in which the word occurs; word forms lemmatized with TreeTagger and POS-tagged, with manual post-processing; (5) remove words under 3 characters, high-frequency function words, names of persons, parties and organizations (AUTNES list), positive words from existing lexicons, and words occurring in only one sentence. Scoring of new texts (Sec. 5): bag-of-words; sentence tonality = most negative dictionary word (max rule); negation word immediately before a dictionary word excludes that word (no polarity flip); intensifier before a word multiplies its score by 1.25, capped at the scale maximum. Validation (Sec. 6, App. 2-3): Pearson correlations with expert and crowd means, coverage, and comparison with two translated German dictionaries (SentiWS, Momtazi). Applications: OLS regression of press-release tonality with government/opposition and coalition-pair indicators, party fixed effects, poll-performance and days-to-election controls, standard errors clustered by party pair (Table 3); descriptive comparison of mean sentence tonality with and without an actor reference, by day (Sec. 7.2, Fig. 6).
extraction.identification: None causal. Observational OLS with party fixed effects and standard errors clustered across party pairs; controls for net poll change and days to election. Robustness is expert-coded dependent variable (App. 3, Table 6).
extraction.scope: Population: German-language political communication in Austria (party press releases, parliamentary debates, and 15 Austrian daily newspapers). Era: corpus 1995-2013; the two applications cover the 2013 national election campaign. Institutions: six parliamentary parties (SPO, OVP, FPO, Greens, BZO, Team Stronach). The procedure is presented as portable to other languages and domains, but no other language or domain is tested.
measures: Negativity/tonality: 0-4 crowd ordinal scale (0 not negative to 4 very strongly negative), aggregated as means of ten coder ratings per sentence
Word tonality score: mean of sentence scores containing the word (range 0.06-3.8 in the 5,001-word dictionary)
Sentence tonality: maximum (most negative) dictionary word score in the sentence (max rule), with negation exclusion and 1.25 intensifier amplification
Validation: Pearson correlation with expert and crowd coding; coverage (share of sentences with a matching dictionary word); binary accuracy 0.85 and F-score 0.91 for negative vs not negative (fn 8)

Application 1 dependent variable: tonality of a directed negative press release statement; independent variables: sender/target/pair government indicators, electoral losses (net poll change), days to election
Application 2: mean sentence tonality for sentences with vs without a party or candidate reference

key_findings.finding: Crowd sentence scores: 480 coders passed the tests with 92% mean accuracy (SD 0.07); about 130,000 valid codings, ten per sentence, for 12,713 sentences; the test-question design implies a 4% chance of passing by guessing.
key_findings.numbers: 480 coders; 92% (SD 0.07); ~130,000 codings; 12,713 sentences; ~2,000 EUR (~2,200 USD)

key_findings.finding: Dictionary scope and size: the rated bag of words falls from about 40,000 initial words to about 5,000 after removing short, frequent, rare, positive, and named-entity words.
key_findings.numbers: 5,001 dictionary words; scores 0.06-3.8 on the 0-4 scale; mean 2.04 (SD 0.65)

key_findings.finding: Lay crowd aggregates replicate expert coding of the 200-sentence test sample, with a slight centrist bias.
key_findings.numbers: Pearson r = 0.82 (aggregated expert vs aggregated crowd, n = 200)

key_findings.finding: Dictionary validity against expert coding: a moderate correlation at 84% coverage. Setting the 32 uncovered sentences to zero lowers the correlation.
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.65, coverage 84% (n = 200); r = 0.6 after assigning zero to 32 uncovered sentences

key_findings.finding: Replication on a larger sample: single expert coding of 755 statements gives similar coverage and correlation; the dictionary-based estimates are described as more conservative than manual-coding estimates.
key_findings.numbers: n = 755; coverage 82%; r = 0.63

key_findings.finding: Generic German dictionaries perform far worse on the same sample, which the authors take as evidence that customization is needed.
key_findings.numbers: Momtazi: r = 0.13, coverage 46%; SentiWS: r = 0.19, coverage 31%; political dictionary: r = 0.65, coverage 84%

key_findings.finding: Preprocessing and aggregation choices matter: stemming alone gives the lowest correlation; the best combination uses lemmatization, POS tagging, stop-word and named-entity deletion, mean word scores, the max rule for sentences, and booster/negation handling.
key_findings.numbers: Table 4 r: stemming 0.13; lemmatizing 0.34; stemming+POS/deletion 0.42; lemmatizing+POS/deletion 0.65 (coverage 84%). Table 5 best: mean word score, max sentence, booster/negation yes: r = 0.65 (n = 168)

key_findings.finding: Application 1, negative campaigning 2013: government parties are less negative than opposition parties, and government-coalition pairs are less negative than other pairs. Electoral losers attack more; no escalation toward the end of the campaign.
key_findings.numbers: Government sender -0.10 (p < 0.05); government pair -0.13 (p < 0.001); electoral losses +0.12 (p < 0.001) in Model 1, not significant in Model 2 (0.10, SE 0.06); proximity -0.01 (n.s.); constant 2.28; n = 619; adjusted R2 = 0.03

key_findings.finding: Application 1 descriptive counts: the three largest parties issue most negative releases. Government parties SPO and OVP and opposition FPO together account for about 4 in 5 negative releases.
key_findings.numbers: 755 negative statements; FPO 232 (30.7%), OVP 199 (26.4%), SPO 164 (21.7%), BZO 68 (9.0%), Greens 59 (7.8%), Team Stronach 33 (4.4%); mean tonality 2.23; dictionary matched 82% of the 755 statements

key_findings.finding: Application 2, media tone: sentences that mention a party or candidate are more negative than sentences that do not. Coverage was slightly negative on average.
key_findings.numbers: 15,096 reports in 15 dailies; 439,954 sentences; about 1 in 5 references an actor; 55% contain a dictionary word (rest coded neutral); mean tonality 1.23 with actor reference vs 1.00 without

key_findings.finding: Appendix 3 check: the sign pattern of the Table 3 coefficients is the same whether scored with the dictionary or with expert coding, but dictionary-based effect sizes are weaker.
key_findings.numbers: Dictionary vs expert, government-pair coefficient -0.13*** vs -0.40***; electoral losses 0.12*** vs 0.23***

limitations: Bag-of-words scoring cannot handle irony, sarcasm, rhetorical questions, or separable verbs; the authors say these are rare enough that coverage is acceptable, but do not measure their share.
Validation rests on 200 sentences rated by two expert authors and ten lay coders, plus a single-coder extension of 755 statements, from one country and language.
Mean aggregation of ordinal ratings produces a centrist bias and decimal scores; the authors acknowledge that purists may object.
Lemmatization and POS tags needed manual cleaning; current German NLP tools were judged unsatisfactory for separable verbs, compounds, dialect and neologisms.
Negation excludes the following word rather than flipping polarity; the procedure focuses on negativity only and does not model positive sentiment.

Non-matching sentences in the media application (45% of sentences) are coded neutral on the assumption that the dictionary covers overtly negative statements; this is not validated for that subset beyond the 200-sentence test.
Application 2 is explicitly illustrative; the authors state it cannot by itself show a critical or cynical journalistic perspective.
Sample size and budget (about 2,000 EUR) were set by a budget limit, not a power calculation.
Reporting inconsistency: Table 2 gives 612 statements with a tonality score, while its party counts sum to 619 and Table 3 reports 619 observations.
Table 3 is text-extracted and its column layout is ambiguous, so the coefficient-to-model assignment above follows the text, not the table grid.
The dictionary's generalization to other domains, languages, or time periods is not tested; the authors recommend custom dictionaries and cautious use of general-purpose ones.

short_quotes.quote: The crowdbased dictionary provides efficient and valid measurement of sentiment.

summary_md:
Haselmayer and Jenny build a negativity dictionary for German-language Austrian political text. About 480 CrowdFlower coders rated 12,713 sentences on a 0-4 negativity scale, ten ratings per sentence, for about 2,000 EUR. Each word's score is the mean score of the sentences it appears in, which yields 5,001 lemmatized words. To score a new sentence, the method takes its single most negative dictionary word (the max rule). A negator drops the word that follows it, and an intensifier multiplies a word's score by 1.25.

Validation on 200 sentences:
- The averaged lay crowd agrees with expert coding at r = 0.82.
- The dictionary agrees with experts at r = 0.65, matching 84% of sentences.
- On 755 statements coded by a single expert, the dictionary gives r = 0.63 at 82% coverage.
- Two translated general-purpose German dictionaries score r = 0.13 and 0.19. The authors read this as evidence that a domain-built dictionary is needed.
- Preprocessing and aggregation choices move r from 0.13 to 0.65.
- In a regression on the 2013 campaign, dictionary scores keep the expert-coded signs but shrink the effects. The government-pair coefficient is -0.13 with the dictionary versus -0.40 with expert coding.

The paper matters here in two places:
1. The live press intensity is stock English Lexicoder LSD2015, scored per release as |net| / words. Its only recorded validation is a three-case smoke test, and it has never been compared with human-coded intensity. The paper's design would supply that test cheaply.
2. Paul's retired graded tone scorer cites this paper by name, but its code departs from the paper. It sums weighted cues across sentences where the paper takes the strongest cue, uses a two-token negator window, adds a downtoner, and uses about 45 hand-weighted patterns rather than crowd-derived word scores.

The evidence is about Austrian German, covers negativity only, and comes from 2013. None of it validates the US congressional tone measures directly.

bearings.paper_claim: Validation on 200 sentences: aggregated lay crowd vs aggregated expert r = 0.82. Domain dictionary vs expert r = 0.65 at 84% coverage, about 0.6 when the 32 unmatched sentences are set to zero. Momtazi r = 0.13 (46% coverage) and SentiWS r = 0.19 (31% coverage). Authors state that dictionary analysis requires a customized dictionary and recommend caution with general-purpose dictionaries.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 6 pp. 2631-2632; Table 1 p. 2633; Conclusion p. 2637; App. 3 p. 2639
bearings.system_side: press_value tone intensity is stock LSD2015, uncustomized. stage5_lsd.R lsd_tone (lines 48-61) removes negator-plus-word hits and flips them: negated negatives count as positive and negated positives as negative. lsd_net_norm = (pos - neg) / words. run_stage5.R line 141 takes abs(lsd_net_norm) as heat; line 143 sets press_value = final_sign x heat. The brain note at debate-stance-model.md line 102 records only a three-case smoke test (pro +4 / negated 0 / neutral 0) and calls LSD validated, (a functional check by the paper standard).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The validation protocol transfers: about 200 releases rated 0-4 by lay coders and experts, correlated with |lsd_net_norm|. The size of the generic-dictionary penalty does not transfer directly, because the paper's comparators are machine-translated German lexicons, not LSD2015. This paper does not establish that LSD2015 performs well on English news; the Young and Soroka citation is general sentiment work, not an LSD validation. The paper scores sentences for negativity only, while LSD here is bidirectional and scores whole release bodies.
bearings.verifier_note: Table and text numbers confirmed (r 0.82, 0.65, 0.6, 84%, 32 sentences, Momtazi 0.13/46%, SentiWS 0.19/31%). The phrase 'each domain needs its own dictionary' overgeneralizes; the paper argues for a customized dictionary for its own domain and language. The system_side negation description is incomplete: negated hits are flipped, not removed. The LSD-validated-on-English-news transfer claim is outside this paper and was not verified.

bearings.paper_claim: Sentence tonality is set by the single most negative dictionary word (max rule). A negator immediately before a word excludes that word, and an intensifier multiplies it by 1.25. Word scores are crowd-derived means on a 0-4 scale. Mean word scores with the max rule and booster/negation handling give r = 0.65 (n = 168 test sentences). Other aggregation combinations give r from 0.38 to 0.58.
bearings.system_side: The graded layer header in cu_press_release_scraper.R cites Haselmayer and Jenny and says sentence tonality follows the strongest cue. The code does not: weighted_tone (about lines 2443-2475) sums every fired cue across all CU sentences into Wp and Wn, and graded_from_signed buckets |Wp - Wn| by GRADED_CUTS. The negator window covers two preceding tokens; a 0.75 downtoner is added (line 139), not in the paper. TONE_LEXICON has 44 hand-weighted entries (weights 1, 2, 3), not crowd-derived scores. run_stage5.R lines 146-160 reuse the magnitude only for display score_label; press_value does not use it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a fidelity finding, not an empirical one. It matters for the display score_label magnitude and the comparison column only, because press_value and the press pillar do not consume the graded layer. No external claim that these graded labels follow Haselmayer and Jenny should be made.

The header line range is slightly off (about 121-132). The relation is a mismatch between the code's citation and the paper, not a paper finding that contradicts the code. Lexicon count is 44 by my count, consistent with 'about 45'.

summary_issues: The summary says the evidence comes from 2013. The corpus spans 1995-2013, the validation sample pools four campaigns from 2002-2013, and only the two applications use the 2013 campaign.

The related link to b-2025-comparing-fine-tuned was removed. That study compares a fine-tuned RoBERTa with TF-IDF classifiers for Roman Urdu stance; it does not test dictionary intensity, so the contradicts relation is not supported.

The summary says the intensity measure is scored as |net| / words. That is correct for the default INTENSITY setting, but net itself flips negated hits rather than removing them (stage5_lsd.R lines 48-61).
Paul's highlight claims and the paul_alignment statements about Birkenmaier and the stale components list were not verified; this item has no Paul entries of its own.
The ext coverage field says Appendices 1-6 were read; the text also has Appendix 7 (CrowdFlower coding task, p. 2640 onward). Minor.
gaps_exposed: The LSD2015 intensity used in press_value has never been correlated with human-coded intensity on congressional press releases. The paper's protocol (about 200 items, a 0-4 scale, about 10 lay coders, 2 experts, reporting r and coverage) is a cheap test the system has not run.

The release-level metric |pos - neg| / words cancels mixed praise and attack, and it penalizes long releases. The paper shows that the aggregation rule alone moves validity (mean vs max; App. 2 Table 5). No alternative aggregation (max per sentence, CU-sentence-only scoring) has been compared.

There is no domain-specific tone dictionary for CU or financial policy. The Rice & Zorn corpus-expansion helper is opt-in and offline, and live scoring uses a generic dictionary, which is the configuration the paper warns about.

LSD hits are counted over the whole release body, not restricted to the sentences that mention credit unions. Releases where LSD finds no tone words get zero intensity, so press_value becomes 0 even when DEBATE assigns a stance. That implicit 'non-match = neutral' rule is the one the paper flags as unvalidated outside its test sample.
No ablation has tested stance sign x intensity against stance sign alone, using a behavioural criterion such as later CU cosponsorship or votes.
flags: CODE/DOC MISMATCH: the header of cu_press_release_scraper.R (lines 125-131) cites Haselmayer & Jenny and says 'Sentence tonality follows the strongest cue', but weighted_tone (lines 2443-2475) sums cues across sentences. The layer is display-only, and run_stage5 4b still uses its magnitude in score_label. Do not describe those labels as following Haselmayer & Jenny.

The brain note debate-stance-model.md:102 calls LSD 'validated' on the basis of a three-case smoke test. By this paper's standard that is a functional check, not a validity result. Under DE-062, any claim that LSD intensity measures how heated a release is should stay UNVERIFIED until it has been compared with human coding.

The paper's Table 3 coefficients are pooled across six parties with party fixed effects. If quoted, label them as from a pooled model with no party strata. Reporting is also inconsistent: Table 2 says 612 statements while its counts sum to 619, the n in Table 3.
Nothing in the paper argues for either rejected SNA proposal, and it does not touch LDA, graph ranks or reciprocity, so there is no conflict with D-021, D-025 or D-104..D-108.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper. It agrees with his highlighted reading of Merkley & Stecula, who used Lexicoder with custom dictionaries: both argue for tailoring dictionaries to the domain, while the system runs stock LSD2015 without customization. His note on Birkenmaier, which calls bag-of-words methods dated next to LLMs, is consistent with the system moving stance to DEBATE. This paper adds a further point: intensity is still bag-of-words, and its validity has never been measured. Paul's earlier graded scorer adopted this paper's vocabulary (ordinal bands, 1.25 amplifier, negator exclusion) but not its max rule or crowd-derived weights. His components list is stale relative to the system in one respect: it says nothing about that departure or about the display-only reuse in run_stage5 4b.

related.why: Both argue for domain-specific sentiment dictionaries. Rice and Zorn derive one from the corpus with word vectors; this paper derives one from crowd ratings. The legacy scorer cites both papers. Verified against the Rice item's research question.

Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder with a custom dictionary to detect party cues, not to measure sentiment intensity. The link is a method precedent for custom dictionaries, not a validation of tone. Verified against the Merkley item text.

Also a domain-lexicon construction method. The rejected bill-sign-handling test (3 good / 43 bad) is claimed in the analyst text and was not checked here; the link rests on the shared point that preprocessing and aggregation choices drive validity.
Offers LLM few-shot coding of political text as an alternative to the crowdcoding step used for intensity gold labels. Verified against the Ornstein item research question.

extraction.title: Influence maximization in social networks: a survey of behaviour-aware methods
extraction.venue: Social Network Analysis and Mining, 13:78 (published online 25 April 2023; received 23 May 2022, revised 12 March 2023, accepted 27 March 2023)
extraction.document_type: Review paper (literature survey with a proposed taxonomy; no empirical study)
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text (all 2,484 lines, about 114k characters, in seven chunks), including front matter, Sections 1 to 4, all four summary tables (Tables 1 to 4, rendered as check-mark grids), author contributions, declarations and the full reference list (pp. 18-21). The metadata hint is correct on title, authors, year, venue and DOI. The text does not discuss lobbying, elections, legislators, text measurement or turnout; the closest content is money-aware (cost and budget) and opinion-aware (trust, opinion) seed selection, covered below. No Paul markup exists: the _annots and annotations folders contain no file matching 0bc326441250, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: No empirical question is posed. The paper asks what behaviour-aware methods for influence maximization (IM) exist in social networks, and proposes to classify and review them as a separate family from behaviour-agnostic, purely structural methods (Sec. 1, pp. 1-3). It also states that previous surveys covered behaviour-agnostic approaches or touched behaviour-aware ones only briefly (p. 2).
extraction.theory: No formal social or economic theory is tested. The framing is IM as discrete optimisation (Eq. 1, p. 4): select a seed set S of size k or under budget B that maximises spread phi(S), with query Q = (M, AM, B) and graph G = (V, E, BV, BE). Behaviour-aware methods use user features BV, relationship features BE and message features AM. Diffusion models are Independent Cascade and Linear Threshold (Kempe et al. 2003; Granovetter 1978), with voter and opinion-formation models used for opinion dynamics.
extraction.data: None. This is a narrative review with no sample, unit of analysis, N or data period. Cited works span roughly 1977 to 2023, but the paper states no explicit inclusion window or search protocol.
extraction.method: Narrative classification and review. The authors propose a two-level taxonomy (pp. 2-5, Fig. 2). Level 1 splits IM methods into behaviour-agnostic and behaviour-aware. Level 2 splits behaviour-aware methods into four families: interest-aware (target-aware, label-aware, topic-aware; Sec. 3.1), opinion-aware (trust-agnostic, trust-aware; Sec. 3.2), money-aware (cost-aware, profit-aware; Sec. 3.3) and physical-world-aware (physical relationship-aware, location-aware; Sec. 3.4). Summary tables code each surveyed paper by behavioural features (AM, BV, BE), influence-detection method (centrality measure CM, spreading simulation SS, reverse influence sampling RIS, maximum influence arborescence MIA) and spreading process type (simple or complex). Section 2.2 ranks influence-detection families by time complexity: simulation-based, then MIA, then RIS, then centrality (p. 4).
extraction.identification: Not applicable. The paper makes no causal or statistical identification claim. It classifies published methods and does not estimate effects.
extraction.scope: Population: social-network IM research, covering online graphs (friendship, follow, trust) and, for physical-world-aware methods, check-in and location-based social networks (Sec. 3.4). No institution or era restriction beyond the cited literature. Behaviour-agnostic methods are explicitly excluded as already surveyed elsewhere (pp. 3, 5).

key_findings.finding: Behaviour-agnostic methods dominate current IM work because they have a longer history, but behaviour-aware formulations are argued to be more realistic. No previous survey had treated behaviour-aware methods as a class of their own.
key_findings.numbers: None; qualitative claim

key_findings.finding: Interest-aware methods split into target-aware (binary interest), label-aware (label sets) and topic-aware (continuous topic vectors). Topic-aware models are judged to capture preferences most realistically but need good historical records. Partly offline topic-aware methods trade offline storage and precomputation for faster online queries.
key_findings.numbers: Table 1 codes the interest-aware papers; no numeric results

key_findings.finding: Opinion-aware methods split into trust-agnostic (all ties positive) and trust-aware (signed friend or foe ties). Trust-agnostic models assume all relationships are positive, which the authors call unrealistic; opinion dynamics under friend and foe influence need more work.
key_findings.numbers: None; Table 2 codes the opinion-aware papers

key_findings.finding: Cost-aware (budgeted) IM assumes every activated user yields the same benefit. Profit-aware methods model per-user benefit and cost, but users' valuations may often be unavailable, so the authors suggest cost-aware methods may be more practical.
key_findings.numbers: Nguyen and Zheng (2013) introduced budgeted IM; Table 3 codes the money-aware papers

key_findings.finding: Physical-world-aware methods add offline ties (co-location, check-in) to the online graph, or use location and attendance probability as the target. Binary physical-tie models and fixed distance thresholds miss the dynamics of user location, and tracking locations over time adds processing and storage cost.
key_findings.numbers: None; qualitative comparison

key_findings.finding: Five open challenge areas are identified: data availability, data processing, data modelling (numeric encodings of attitude and friend or foe ties), data dynamicity, and user reaction modelling. Research directions cover network size and time complexity, network diversity (temporal, multilayer, dynamic), data preparation, and adaptive diffusion models that feed behaviour changes back into spread.
key_findings.numbers: None

measures: Not applicable to the paper's own analysis. Reviewed methods use centrality measures, spreading simulation, reverse influence sampling (Borgs et al. 2012) and maximum influence arborescence (Chen et al. 2010). Tables 1-4 code features as AM, BV, BE and detection as CM, SS, RIS or MIA, with simple or complex spreading.
limitations: The paper states no methodological limitations of its own review: no search protocol, inclusion rule, or count of surveyed papers.
Stated scope limit: it reviews behaviour-aware methods only and defers behaviour-agnostic methods to earlier surveys (pp. 3, 5).
Stated challenge: behaviour data may not exist, may be incomplete or noisy, or may be governed by privacy rules (Sec. 4, p. 17).
Stated challenge: many behaviour-aware models encode attitudes and friend or foe ties as numbers, which may not capture personality or attitude (Sec. 4, p. 17).
Stated challenge: most methods use conventional IC or LT diffusion models that may not emulate real spreading; changing the model can significantly change accuracy (Sec. 4, p. 18).
The paper classifies methods and does not benchmark or compare their accuracy.

summary_md:
Zareie and Sakellariou (2023, SNAM 13:78) is a narrative survey with no data. It proposes a two-level taxonomy of influence maximization (IM). Level 1 separates behaviour-agnostic methods, which use structure only, from behaviour-aware methods. Level 2 splits behaviour-aware methods into four families: interest-aware (target, label, topic), opinion-aware (trust-agnostic vs signed friend/foe), money-aware (cost-aware budgeted IM vs profit-aware) and physical-world-aware. Tables 1-4 code each surveyed method by which features it uses: message (AM), user (BV) or relationship (BE). They also code how it detects influence (centrality, simulation, RIS or MIA) and whether spreading is simple or complex. The useful content is qualitative. Topic-aware edge probabilities are judged the most realistic, but they need rich history. Trust-agnostic models, which treat every tie as positive, are called unrealistic. Profit-aware IM needs per-user valuations that are rarely available, so cost-aware IM may be more practical. The authors also warn that changing the diffusion model can change accuracy a lot, and that many users are silent.

For Melange the paper is mainly a lens on design choices that were already made. The code cites it directly: receptivity_layer.py:29-31 and outcome_contract.py:17 ('Chen/SNAM') use it to back contingency-aware seeding. But the survey gives no estimate of seed take-up and no magnitudes, so it supports only the general idea that member features belong in IM. Against the built engine, the survey exposes three choices. First, one topic-independent cascade kernel serves all 18 CU categories. Second, the kernel is trust-agnostic: partisan factors change edge magnitude, never sign, and the signed reference layer is display-only. Third, the optimizer has a profit-aware shape, weighting members by owner-set values (PERS, IMP), which is the exact data the survey calls usually unavailable. All of these are design-level bearings. Nothing in the paper validates or refutes any constant in the system.

bearings.paper_claim: Behaviour-aware IM adds user features (BV), relationship features (BE) and message features (AM) to the structural IM problem (Eq. 1). The survey reports no take-up rate, no effect size and no benchmark, and it classifies methods without comparing their accuracy. It warns that numeric encodings of attitude may not capture personality and that many users are silent.

The survey says this captures preferences more realistically than binary target or label methods, but determining topic vectors needs a good record of historical activity, which may not always be available. The survey reports no accuracy comparison of any kind.

The recorded crypto p_max of 0.23 was not checked.

Trust-aware work uses signed graphs on the premise that opinion change depends on trust between users. The survey also warns that numeric friend-or-foe encodings may not capture attitude.

The signed member-reference (LLM valence) layer is stated to be display-only; that was not checked.

The survey's warning on numeric attitude encodings applies to the LLM valence scores. Signed edges would also change the two-physics architecture, so the owner decides.

meta.title: Detecting coalitions by optimally partitioning signed networks of political collaboration

extraction.title: Detecting coalitions by optimally partitioning signed networks of political collaboration
extraction.coverage: Full text read end to end from the extracted file (all journal pages 1-10 including the abstract, introduction, signed-graph preliminaries, bounding and computation sections, results, conclusions, methods, data availability and the 52-item reference list). Metadata hint was correct. Figures 1-6 were read from their captions and surrounding text only; plotted values were not visible in the extraction. Supplementary Information (Tables S2, S4 and data/code) is referenced but was not in the file and was not read. No Paul markup files existed for this PDF, so paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: Can the members of internally cohesive, mutually antagonistic coalitions in a signed network of legislators be identified exactly by optimally partitioning the network to minimize frustration? And does the partisan composition of the largest such coalition explain changes in legislative effectiveness (bill passage) better than party control or party affiliation does?
extraction.theory: Structural balance theory (Heider 1944; Cartwright and Harary 1956), with the frustration index (Harary 1959) as the global balance measure, and coalition theory (Riker 1962). Substantive framing draws on the legislative effectiveness literature (Volden and Wiseman; Frantzich; Olson and Nonidez) and on Mayhew's claim that parties are not sufficient analytic units. Central substantive hypothesis: a more partisan, ideologically unified controlling coalition improves passage rates (protective factor), while party majority size does not.
extraction.data: Signed networks of US House and Senate members, one network per chamber per Congressional session, sessions 96th to 114th (1979-2016), i.e. 19 sessions per chamber and about 38 networks (derived count). Edges are signed dyads built from bill co-sponsorship: a negative edge is a dyad whose joint co-sponsorships are significantly few under a stochastic degree sequence model null (two-tailed alpha 0.05); a positive edge is significantly many. Unit of analysis: legislator dyads within a session-chamber network, with session-level aggregates for the regressions. Network data are from Neal (2019, figshare, reference 4). Legislator counts per chamber are not stated in the main text. Example scale: the 113th House graph has m = 75,771 edges and 7,102,625 triangles. Pre-96th sessions were excluded because of the 25-cosponsor House rule before 1979. Bill passage rate is the share of introduced bills that become law, per chamber per session. Party data come from exogenous legislator party affiliation. The printed size bound for the dense-graph method appears as "|E| ... 50000" with the relation symbol lost in extraction, so the exact bound is unverified.
extraction.method: Two partial-balance measures on each network: the triangle index T(G) (Eq. 3, trace-based, fraction of positive triangles) and the normalized frustration index F(G) = 1 - 2L(G)/m (Eq. 6), where L(G) is the frustration index, i.e. the minimum number of intra-group negative plus inter-group positive edges over all two-group partitions (Eqs. 4-5). Exact computation uses (a) a continuous LP relaxation with triangle inequality constraints (Eq. 7) to give a lower bound Y*, solved in Gurobi 8.0; (b) a warm start that initializes each node's group from party affiliation, which also gives an upper bound; and (c) a binary linear program (Eq. 8, XOR-style frustration variables with the lower bound added as a constraint) that returns the exact frustration index and the optimal partition X*. The larger side of X* is the controlling coalition, and coalition partisanship is the fraction of its non-independent members who belong to its dominant party. Inference is cross-sectional, session by session. Two models: a commonsense model (party control = absolute difference between Republican and Democratic seat counts) and a coalition model (coalition partisanship). Each is estimated as a structural equation mediation model with time as the predictor and passage rate as the outcome, using bivariate regressions and standardized betas (unstandardized percentage-point slopes reported for context).
extraction.identification: None causal. The mediation models use time and session-level cross-sections, so the indirect effect (time to coalition partisanship to passage rate) is a statistical decomposition, not an identified causal effect. Exogenous party labels are used to warm-start the solver and as a comparison benchmark, not as an instrument.
extraction.scope: US Congress (House and Senate), 96th-114th sessions, 1979-2016. Population is legislators in co-sponsorship networks; the inferred ties cover only that period. Results are claimed for the House only on the effectiveness question; the Senate shows no support for the coalition model. The computational method is general to signed graphs with up to a stated dense-graph size. The Senate networks are small enough that exact solves took 4 seconds on average.

key_findings.finding: Triangle index and normalized frustration index both show high partial balance that rose over 1979-2016 in both chambers, read as increasing polarization. The two measures are highly correlated.
key_findings.numbers: Correlation of T(G) and F(G) is 0.95 for the House and 0.91 for the Senate (as printed, 'respectively for House and Senate').

key_findings.finding: Exact frustration index and optimal partition are computable for dense House networks, but the cost is large. The Senate is cheap.
key_findings.numbers: 113th House: LP bound (Eq. 7) takes 5,300 s with 28,486,271 constraints; binary model (Eq. 8) has n+m = 76,218 binary variables and 2m+1 = 151,543 constraints and takes 43,523 s; total 48,823 s (about 13.5 h), the longest House instance. House average 17,763 s (SD 15,411 s). Senate average 4 s (SD 6 s).

key_findings.finding: Controlling coalitions (largest side of the optimal partition) became more partisan (more homogeneous) over 1979-2016 in both chambers.
key_findings.location: Results, Partial balance and optimal partitioning (p.6), Fig. 3
key_findings.numbers: No regression coefficient reported in the text for this descriptive trend; Fig. 3 shows counts of the two main parties in the controlling coalition.

key_findings.finding: Bill passage rates declined over time in both chambers.
key_findings.location: Results, Mediation in bill passage (p.6), Fig. 5(A)
key_findings.numbers: House: -0.11 percentage points per session (standardized beta = -0.528, p < 0.05). Senate: -0.35 percentage points per session (beta = -0.852, p < 0.01).

key_findings.finding: The commonsense explanation fails: party control (absolute majority size) does not mediate the time-passage relation in either chamber.
key_findings.numbers: No significant mediation reported; text says party control does not mediate the relationship between time and passage rate.

key_findings.finding: In the House, coalition partisanship mediates the decline in passage rates. Greater partisan homogeneity of the controlling coalition is a protective factor, so the decline would have been worse without it.
key_findings.numbers: Time to coalition partisanship: beta = 0.771, p < 0.01. Coalition partisanship to passage: beta = 0.661, p < 0.05. Indirect effect of time on passage via coalition partisanship: beta = 0.510, p < 0.05. Direct effect: beta = -1.038, p < 0.01 (as printed; a standardized beta above 1 in magnitude is unusual, so verify against Fig. 5(C)).

key_findings.finding: The coalition-partisanship mediation is not supported in the Senate. The authors tie this to Senate procedure, where lack of majority control of procedure negates party or group effects.
key_findings.location: Results (p.7); Conclusions (p.8), citing Monroe, Roberts and Rohde (ref 43)
key_findings.numbers: No significant Senate mediation effect reported.

key_findings.finding: The composition of the largest cohesive coalition matters more than the size of the majority party's majority in a chamber where a large group can shape procedure. The authors frame this as a claim about analytic units beyond parties.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative conclusion; no additional statistics.

limitations: The paper has no separate limitations section. Limits stated in the text: (1) legislator ties are inferred from co-sponsorship and are not observed collaboration; co-sponsorship can also indicate avoidance (p.8). (2) Networks are analyzed cross-sectionally, one per session, because of joiners and leavers and the difficulty of estimating dynamic models; the authors argue each session's effectiveness can be evaluated independently (p.9). (3) Pre-96th sessions are excluded because of the 25-cosponsor House rule, and the co-sponsor data do not separate sponsors from co-sponsors (p.8-9). (4) The coalition effect holds only for the House, not the Senate (p.8). (5) The exact method is computationally heavy for large House graphs (13.5 h for one instance), and the authors note heuristic methods are not guaranteed to be optimal (p.2). (6) The mediation models are bivariate and session-level, so they support association and not causation. (7) Figure values and the large direct-effect coefficient (beta = -1.038) were read from captions and printed text only and should be checked against the figures and supplement.

summary_md:
Aref and Neal build one signed network per chamber per Congress (96th to 114th, 1979-2016). Each network comes from a stochastic-degree-sequence (SDSM) backbone of bill cosponsorship: a dyad that cosponsors together significantly more often than the null predicts gets a positive edge, and one that does so significantly less often gets a negative edge. They then solve the two-group frustration-minimization problem exactly. An LP relaxation with triangle constraints gives a lower bound, a party-label warm start gives an upper bound, and a binary program returns the exact frustration index and the optimal partition. Both balance measures are high and rising over the period (the triangle and normalized frustration indices correlate at 0.95 in the House and 0.91 in the Senate), which the authors read as polarization. Exact solves are cheap for the Senate (about 4 s) and expensive for the House (up to about 13.5 h for the 113th Congress, which has 75,771 edges). The larger side of the optimal partition, the controlling coalition, became more partisan over time. In session-level bivariate mediation models (19 sessions per chamber; association, not cause), coalition partisanship partly offsets the House decline in passage rates (indirect beta 0.510). Majority size does not mediate it, and the Senate shows no effect.

For Paul's systems the paper matters mainly for the diagnostic signed-coalition layer. That layer cites the 2021 follow-up, runs a heuristic local search with no lower bound on an LLM-valenced mention graph, and pools both chambers. At its size (520 members, 7,153 edges) the paper's exact binary program looks tractable. That estimate is derived here and is UNVERIFIED. The paper also gives an outside reading of the project's earlier result that a vote SDSM backbone is about 95% party: under structural balance that is expected, not a defect. It does not license the SDSM null as a fix for the network's degree artifact. That would amount to the per-edge volume normalization the project already measured and rejected.

The 113th House (m = 75,771) takes 48,823 s: 5,300 s for the LP (28,486,271 constraints) and 43,523 s for the binary solve.

extraction.title: Characterizing equitable access to grocery stores during disasters using location-based data
extraction.venue: Scientific Reports 12:20203 (Nature Portfolio, open access CC BY 4.0). Received 27 April 2022, accepted 31 October 2022.
extraction.document_type: Empirical journal article (location-based mobility data, network analysis and time-series clustering)
extraction.coverage: Full text read in one pass (all 938 lines of _text/c82f74711258.txt): front matter, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, data and code availability, 51 references, funding and author notes. Metadata hint confirmed (title, authors, 2022, Scientific Reports, DOI all match the PDF text). Paul's markup: no markup files were listed for this item, so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or sticky notes were checked. Page numbers are inferred from the journal page-number lines in the extracted text and should be checked against the PDF. Coverage of the lobbying, elections, persuasion/turnout, legislator and text-measurement topics: none of these appear in the paper. Its network content is limited to population-facility (TAZ-to-store) trip networks and accessibility metrics.
extraction.research_question: (1) What are the characteristics of access to grocery stores for different sub-populations at different stages of disasters? (2) What is the extent of disparity in access among different sociodemographic groups in different disaster phases? (3) What are the contributing factors to unequal access to grocery stores, and to what extent are facility distribution inequities, such as food deserts, indicative of access disparities? (p.2, lines 106-112)
extraction.theory: Access to facilities is treated as three complementary dimensions: redundancy (number of distinct stores visited), rapidity (trip duration, reflecting traffic and road disruption and restoration of system function), and proximity (trip distance). The paper argues that physical-distance and food-desert measures are inadequate in disasters because disruption changes store availability and trip time, and because household capabilities and protective behavior shape access. Framing draws on accessibility and resilience literature (refs 6, 22-28, 33-35). It is not a formal behavioral or economic theory.
extraction.data: Unit of analysis: census-tract-aggregated traffic analysis zones (TAZs) as population nodes, linked to grocery points-of-interest (POIs) as facility nodes. Sample: 1,804 TAZs, 920 grocery stores, 6,052 TAZ-POI links in Harris County, Texas (Fig. 2a caption, p.4). Period: StreetLight O-D trips for 1 Aug to 30 Sep 2017. Analysis window 1 Aug to 15 Sep 2017 (p.6). Baseline 1-20 Aug 2017 (weekday-matched). Normal-period clustering window is stated as 5-16 Aug in the text and 7-16 Aug in the Fig. 3 caption, so it is inconsistent. Sources: StreetLight Data (anonymized cell and GPS trips, not individual-level counts reported; the paper cites more than 40 billion records nationally per month); SafeGraph POIs (grocery, specialty food and general merchandise categories, manually filtered); ACS 2015-2019 5-year estimates; FEMA Harvey flood depth grid; USDA Food Access Research Atlas. The StreetLight penetration rate is given as "approximately 23 penetration rate" in the extracted text, which appears garbled and should be verified in the PDF. Data access is restricted by license and code is available on request.
extraction.method:
Descriptive population-facility network analysis plus unsupervised time-series clustering. (1) Build directed bipartite TAZ-to-POI networks (unweighted; weighted by trip duration; weighted by trip distance) from daily aggregated trips (Table 1, Eqs. 1-3). (2) Compute three TAZ-level indicators: unweighted degree (unique POIs visited), average weighted degree for duration (seconds), and average weighted degree for distance (miles). (3) Express each indicator as percentage change from the weekday baseline, Pc = (M - B)/B (Eq. 4, p.5). (4) Impute gaps with a Kalman filter via R imputeTS after dropping TAZs with 5+ consecutive missing days. (5) Smooth with a 3-day moving average, then run partitional multivariate DTW clustering (dtwclust, R). Cluster number is chosen with COP and modified Davies-Bouldin indices, and the chosen k and the cluster sizes are not reported in the text. (6) Compare sociodemographic and facility characteristics across clusters and income groups (ANOVA, Tukey, chi-square, a two-sample proportion test, and a correlation between number of POIs in a TAZ and each percentage change). Phases: normal (pre-event), preparation (single focal day 24 Aug 2017, the largest percentage change, before landfall on 25 Aug), and impact/short-term recovery (flood-affected TAZs). Flooded TAZ = flood extent above 6.5% of TAZ area (the 75th percentile in Harris County).</method>
<parameter name="identification">None. The study is descriptive and associational. Group comparisons (income tertiles, food-desert status, clusters) and phase comparisons are not causal. The paper uses causal language in places ("disproportionately exacerbated", "flooding disproportionally affects"), which the design does not support. The text mentions a "multivariate analysis" (p.13) but no model, coefficients or specification are reported.
extraction.scope: Population: residents of Harris County, Texas (Houston metro), identified by home TAZ, who visited grocery stores in August-September 2017. Institutions: grocery stores and supermarkets (including warehouse clubs, supercenters and eating places in the category filter). Era: a single event, Hurricane Harvey (landfall 25 Aug 2017, over 60 inches of rain). Single county, single storm, single month window. The paper's own claim about generalizing beyond this event is not present.

key_findings.finding: Normal-period clusters on the three access indicators show spatial clustering, and the three sets of clusters barely overlap. Areas with low redundancy are concentrated in the east and south of the county, and large northern TAZs have poor proximity and rapidity.
key_findings.numbers: Three clusters per indicator; Fig. 3d shows group counts in parentheses, which are not extracted in the text.

key_findings.finding: The normal-period cluster with the highest redundancy is described as lower socioeconomic status. This conflicts with the Table 3 values as extracted (see limitations).
key_findings.numbers: Table 3 extracted: per-capita income for the highest-redundancy cluster C1 = $36,008.19 (starred, significant) vs $28,305.49 and $28,305.94; food-desert share 0.45* vs 0.38 and 0.34; stores per TAZ 0.67 vs 1.03 and 1.87*.

key_findings.finding: Preparation phase (24 Aug 2017): high-income TAZs had a significantly larger increase in unique stores visited than low-income TAZs (ANOVA and Tukey, alpha 0.05). Lower-income TAZs with long normal-period trips had a disproportionately larger increase in trip duration. High-income TAZs with short normal-period distances had the largest increase in distance.
key_findings.numbers: No effect sizes, means or test statistics for these comparisons appear in the text, only boxplots.

key_findings.finding: Correlation between number of POIs in a TAZ and each percentage change in access indicators during preparation is very weak. The text reads it as a slight association for redundancy only, and no association for duration or distance.
key_findings.numbers: Visited-POI % change r = -0.06, p = 0.007; duration % change r = -0.01, p = 0.448; distance % change r = -0.03, p = 0.100.

key_findings.finding: Within food deserts, high-income TAZs visited more POIs during preparation without significantly longer trips or distances than low-income TAZs in food deserts. The authors conclude food-desert status alone does not capture preparation access.
key_findings.location: Results, income x food desert, pp.9-10 (lines 630-657; Fig. 5)
key_findings.numbers: No counts or test statistics for the four income x food-desert groups in the text.

key_findings.finding: Among flood-affected TAZs during impact and short-term recovery, two access clusters emerge. Cluster 2 shows a larger increase in unique POIs visited and a smaller loss of proximity and rapidity. Cluster 2 has higher income, a lower minority share, a higher chance of food-desert status, and fewer POIs per TAZ.
key_findings.numbers: Two clusters; cluster sizes not reported in the text.

key_findings.finding: Income and food-desert status interact in the recovery clusters. Among cluster 2 TAZs, high-income TAZs are a larger share of food-desert TAZs than low-income ones. This pattern is absent in cluster 1.
key_findings.numbers: Cluster 2: high-income share in food deserts 0.53 vs low-income 0.25 (p < 0.001). Cluster 1: 0.57 vs 0.47 (p = 0.76).

key_findings.finding: Flood extent does not differ significantly between the two recovery clusters. The authors argue that diminished access extends beyond flooding and is explained by sociodemographic and facility-distribution characteristics. This works against the abstract's claim that flooding disproportionally affects socially vulnerable populations.
key_findings.numbers: p = 0.33 for flooding extent, cluster 1 vs cluster 2; flood threshold 6.5% of TAZ area.

key_findings.finding: Discussion conclusion: during recovery, higher-income, lower-minority areas kept higher redundancy with smaller losses in proximity and rapidity. Lower-income, higher-minority areas had longer commutes and fewer store visits.
key_findings.numbers: None beyond the results above.

summary_md:
Esmalian et al. use StreetLight origin-destination trips and SafeGraph store locations to build bipartite networks linking traffic zones to grocery stores in Harris County during Hurricane Harvey (Aug-Sep 2017). The sample is 1,804 zones, 920 stores and 6,052 links. Each zone gets three access measures: redundancy (how many distinct stores its residents visit), rapidity (mean trip time) and proximity (mean trip distance). Each measure is expressed as percentage change from a weekday baseline and clustered with dynamic time warping (DTW).

In the preparation phase, high-income zones added more distinct stores than low-income zones. During recovery, the cluster that held up better had higher incomes and a lower minority share. The number of stores in a zone barely tracks the change in access: r = -0.06 for stores visited, -0.01 for trip time and -0.03 for trip distance. Food-desert status alone does not separate the groups. The paper's own test finds no flood-extent difference between the recovery clusters (p = 0.33), which undercuts the abstract's flooding claim.

The design is descriptive: one storm, one county, about six weeks. It reports no effect sizes. As extracted, Table 3 contradicts the text about which cluster is lower-income.

For Paul's systems this is an Adjacent paper with almost no transfer. It says nothing about lobbying, legislators, persuasion, turnout or influence networks. Its "network degree" counts distinct stores visited; it is not a centrality or influence measure. The only real point of contact: counting facilities on the supply side, or measuring plain distance, is a weak stand-in for the access people actually get. That bears weakly on Demographic Potential v3.0, which scores CU branch share and deposit share as "potential". It bears more weakly still on the Terrier turf planner, which ranks blocks by walking distance. Both transfers are by analogy across domains (grocery stores in a disaster vs CU branches and canvass walks in normal conditions). They are UNVERIFIED as evidence for either component.

bearings.paper_claim: How many facilities a zone has is a poor indicator of realized access. Correlation of stores per zone with the preparation-phase % change: stores visited r = -0.06 (p = 0.007), trip time r = -0.01 (p = 0.448), trip distance r = -0.03 (p = 0.100). Window: 24 Aug 2017. Denominator: Harris County zones in the analysis, N not reported. Food-desert status alone did not separate high- from low-income access.

bearings.system_side: The default Demographic Potential (footprint, ruling R7, D-035) scores a district on supply-side presence. Weights: CU employment LQ .30, establishment LQ .20, CU branch share .25, CU deposit share .25. It treats current footprint as the potential and makes no use-based or access-based measure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak analogy only. The paper covers grocery trips in a disaster in one county, with access measured from mobility traces. Demographic Potential is a national, district-level market score under normal conditions. It is explicitly not a measure of support or access, and the footprint choice is an owner ruling. The paper's lesson (supply counts are not realized use) would matter only if footprint were read as members' or constituents' access to CUs. It does not challenge the owner's choice to treat footprint as potential. The same caution applies to the growth_room branch-whitespace term (demographic_potential.py:152).

gaps_exposed: Demographic Potential (footprint v3.0 and growth_room v2.1) uses only supply-side measures: branch and deposit share, LQ and whitespace. It has no measure of realized use, such as CU visits or membership per resident, to test whether presence equals access. The paper shows that facility counts track use changes only weakly (|r| <= 0.06). This matters only if footprint is ever read as access.

No component checks whether its scores differ across sociodemographic strata such as income or minority share. The paper's main finding is heterogeneity by income tertile. Any future use of a pooled district score over income strata should be quoted with those strata or labelled UNSTRATIFIED.
flags: The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Its 'networks' are bipartite zone-to-store trip graphs, and 'degree' means distinct stores visited, not influence, closeness or access probability. Do not port its 'weighted degree' language into Melange SNA wording (D-025).

The causal language in the paper ('disproportionately exacerbated', 'flooding disproportionally affects') is not supported by its descriptive design, and its own test finds no flood-extent difference between clusters (p = 0.33). Do not cite it for causal claims.
As extracted, Table 3 contradicts the text: the highest-redundancy cluster shows a higher per-capita income ($36,008, starred) and fewer stores (0.67). Check against the PDF before quoting.
The normal-period window is inconsistent: 5-16 Aug in the text vs 7-16 Aug in the Fig. 3 caption. Any figure quoted from it must name which window it uses.
Both bearings are this agent's analogy across domains. They stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper, and no component lists it among his citations. Nothing in his positions to agree or disagree with, and no stale note to update. His one related idea is the state or industry-presence targeting layer, which became Demographic Potential (Huneeus & Kim). The paper gently cautions that presence differs from realized access. It does not touch the owner ruling that footprint is the potential.

related.why: Hargittai documents sampling biases in big data drawn from digital traces. Esmalian rests on StreetLight cell/GPS traces with an undescribed penetration rate and black-box home-zone inference, which is exactly that kind of bias. Read together, this limits how far its findings by income can be trusted.

Both papers infer movement cost or access from observed movement rather than straight-line distance: Zeller estimates resistance to movement with step and path selection functions, and Esmalian uses trip time vs trip distance. Both are relevant to any travel-cost weighting in the Terrier turf planner.

meta.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization

extraction.title: Heuristic centrality methods challenge greedy optimization in influence maximization
extraction.document_type: Journal article: empirical comparative study of eight influence maximization algorithms on simulated Independent Cascade diffusion over Facebook subgraphs (open access, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0)
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (1352 lines, about 91k characters, pages 1-18 including references and declarations) in four 250-line chunks plus a final chunk; no section skipped. Metadata hint checked against the text: title, authors, venue, DOI and year all match, so no correction was needed. paul_markup is empty because the task listed no markup files; no sidecar or annotation files were searched for or read. The text is a PDF extraction, so page numbers are inferred from running footers (page 1 = lines 1-46; page 8 = lines 455-551; page 15 = lines 1081-1148).
extraction.research_question: Do the theoretical guarantees of influence maximization algorithms (greedy CELF++, sampling-based RIS and IMM) hold in practice, and how do they compare with simple centrality heuristics (Degree, PageRank, Betweenness, Dangling, GCCDC) on spread quality, runtime and scaling under the Independent Cascade model on real social network subgraphs?
extraction.theory: Influence maximization is NP-hard under IC and LT (Kempe et al. 2003, ref 12). The influence function is submodular, so greedy selection gives a (1-1/e) approximation (Nemhauser et al. 1978, ref 15). CELF and CELF++ use lazy evaluation to speed up greedy without changing that guarantee. RIS and IMM recast the problem as coverage of reverse-reachable sets with sampling bounds. Centrality heuristics carry no guarantee and are justified as cheap structural proxies. The paper's framing: asymptotic guarantees can diverge from practice because hidden constants, network structure and implementation matter (p.4, lines 260-269; p.13, lines 948-961).
extraction.data: Source: Facebook ego network from the SNAP collection, 4,039 nodes and 88,234 undirected edges (p.6, lines 402-404). Sampled subgraphs: 200, 500, 800 and 1000 nodes per Methods and Table 2 (p.6, p.8); the abstract instead says 200, 400, 600, 800 and 1,000 nodes (p.1). Unit: one seed set per algorithm, size and run. Count: 8 algorithms x 4 sizes x 10 independent runs (seeds 42-51) = 320 seed sets, each scored by 50 Monte Carlo IC simulations (p.6, lines 411-434). No time period; a static snapshot of the 2014 SNAP dataset.
extraction.method: Eight algorithms, implemented in Python 3.8 with NumPy 1.21 and NetworkX 2.6 (p.8): CELF++ (50 MC per marginal-gain estimate); RIS with theta = min(10000, 50n); IMM with epsilon = 0.2; Degree; PageRank (damping 0.85, power iteration, tolerance 1e-6, max 100 iterations); Betweenness (Brandes); Dangling centrality; GCCDC (p.4-6). Diffusion: IC with uniform p = 0.1 on all edges; seed budget k = 10. Subgraphs drawn by importance sampling: node importance is the average of normalised degree centrality and normalised PageRank; top-ranked nodes plus their highest-importance neighbours are kept to keep the subgraph connected (p.6, lines 402-410). Evaluation: mean spread over 50 MC simulations per seed set; 10 runs per configuration; mean, SD, min, max and CV reported; wall-clock seconds; spread per second as efficiency (p.7-8). Significance: paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction (alpha 0.05), with Mann-Whitney U said to give the same results (p.7-8, p.8).
extraction.identification: None in a causal sense. This is a controlled simulation benchmark: algorithms are compared on identical subgraphs under the same IC settings, and seeds are paired across runs for the t-tests. No natural experiment or instrument is used.
extraction.scope: One real-world network (Facebook ego network subgraphs) at 200-1000 nodes; one diffusion model (IC, uniform p = 0.1); one seed budget (k = 10); undirected graphs only. Not tested: directed, weighted or temporal networks; other diffusion models; large-scale graphs; deep RL or GNN methods. The paper says the sampled subgraphs have degree exponent above 3 (p.6, lines 408-409).

key_findings.finding: CELF++ performs far below the other algorithms at 1000 nodes (about 12.9% of IMM), despite its (1-1/e) guarantee. The authors attribute this mainly to only 50 MC simulations per estimate and Python implementation, not to an algorithmic flaw.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 473-486); Discussion p.13 (lines 948-955); Conclusion p.15-16
key_findings.numbers: CELF++ 122.95 +/- 24.37 vs IMM 954.90 +/- 1.27; ratio 12.9%; Delta 831.95, t = -107.78, p < 0.001. Abstract (p.1) says 11.2%, which conflicts.

key_findings.finding: IMM is best at 1000 nodes and RIS is close behind. The IMM-RIS gap is small but significant.
PageRank and Betweenness are statistically indistinguishable and reach about 96.5% of IMM spread at 1000 nodes, at 0.4 s and 8.8 s respectively.
key_findings.location: Results p.8-9 (lines 474-476, 495-499); Table 3 p.11; efficiency p.10 (lines 658-666); Discussion p.13 and p.15
key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 +/- 3.28; Betweenness 921.80 +/- 3.34; Delta -0.02, t = -0.01, p = 0.99; PageRank vs IMM Delta 33.12, t = 26.97, p < 0.001. The paper states 96.3% in the abstract, Discussion and Conclusion, but 921.78/954.90 = 96.5%. Stated 794x runtime speed-up: 323.5/0.4 = 809x from the paper's own times.

key_findings.finding: Degree, GCCDC and Dangling form a lower cluster around 80-85% of IMM spread. Dangling is lowest. GCCDC does not improve on Degree at 1000 nodes.
key_findings.location: Results p.8 (lines 475-477); Algorithm-specific observations p.12 (lines 893-908); Broader Discussion p.15 (lines 1123-1129)
key_findings.numbers: Degree 810.87 +/- 6.77; GCCDC 811.59 +/- 5.00; Dangling 797.44 +/- 12.05 (CV up to 6.24%). Degree vs Dangling t = 2.67, p < 0.05; GCCDC vs Dangling t = 2.90, p < 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Sampling methods (IMM, RIS) have very low variance and scale near-linearly. Heuristics have moderate CVs. CELF++ is unstable, with a non-monotone trajectory.
key_findings.location: Scalability p.9 (lines 558-576); Algorithm-specific observations p.11-12 (lines 868-875); Fig. 4 p.10
key_findings.numbers: IMM CV 0.07-0.17%; RIS CV 0.13-0.23%; Betweenness CV 0.16-0.36%; PageRank 0.14-0.25%; Degree 0.66-2.59%; CELF++ CV rose to 71.5% at 500 nodes (p.10, line 646).

key_findings.numbers: Text: IMM +402%, RIS +399%, PageRank +403%, Degree +411%, CELF++ +633%. Table 4: IMM +402%, RIS +400%, PageRank +404%, Degree +410%, CELF++ +740%. CELF++ at 500 nodes is 4.56 in the text and 4.91 in Table 2.

key_findings.numbers: PageRank 921.78 spread / 0.4 s; IMM 954.90 / 323.5 s; CELF++ 122.95 / 688.4 s max runtime. RIS vs PageRank: 3.3% lower spread for 162x runtime (p.10-11).

key_findings.finding: Extrapolated runtimes to 10,000 nodes are reported but were not measured.
key_findings.numbers: RIS about 795 s; IMM about 3970 s; CELF++ about 840 s at 1000 nodes and over 8,400 s at 10,000 nodes (linear extrapolation). The limitations section also quotes PageRank at about 5 s at 10,000 nodes, a figure not given in the Discussion. Linear scaling from RIS's 64.9 s would give about 649 s, not 795 s.

Across 10 runs: mean, SD, min, max, coefficient of variation

Stated: uniform IC probability p = 0.1 only, with no weighted-cascade or LT model; the authors expect ranking changes under other models.
Stated: a single seed budget (k = 10); behaviour at k = 1-3 or k > 50 is not tested.
Stated: scales limited to 200-1000 nodes; results at millions to billions of nodes are extrapolated and not validated.

Stated: CELF++ used only 50 MC simulations per estimate versus 10,000+ in practice, using a Python 3.8 implementation; the authors say the underperformance is likely a budget and implementation artefact, not a flaw in the algorithm.

Stated: importance-based sampling (top degree and PageRank nodes) may densify the subgraph around hubs and favour centrality heuristics; the authors claim robustness to the extraction method without testing it.

summary_md:
Almazaydeh et al. compare eight influence-maximization methods under the Independent Cascade (IC) model. The graphs are Facebook ego-network subgraphs of 200 to 1,000 nodes, with uniform p = 0.1, k = 10 seeds, 10 runs and 50 Monte Carlo (MC) simulations per seed set. At 1,000 nodes, IMM is best (954.90) and RIS is close behind (952.53, five times faster). PageRank and Betweenness cannot be told apart (about 921.8, or 96.5% of IMM; the paper itself says 96.3%), and PageRank runs in 0.4 s. Degree, GCCDC and Dangling reach about 80-85% of IMM. CELF++ collapses to 12.9% of IMM (the abstract says 11.2%), with a CV of up to 71.5%. The authors blame only 50 MC simulations per marginal estimate plus a Python implementation, but they never test that explanation. The study has several internal inconsistencies: subgraph sizes, percentages, the 794x speed-up and the extrapolated runtimes do not match the paper's own tables.

This paper is already wired into Melange. `fec/engine/mc_stability_check.py` names it as its motivation. The skill library cites it to argue that the frontier's MC=20 greedy is safe because common random numbers (CRN) mean every candidate is compared under the same draws. That reasoning is sound for comparing marginals. The problem is that the recorded pass is older than a 2026-10-01 fix. The pass (MEA-7, holistic graph: 100% at MC=100, 98% across RNG seeds) was measured before QME fix 3. Before that fix, the splitmix keys did not depend on SEED, so the 'different RNG seed' runs reused the same edge and seed-activation draws. The MC=100 leg still holds, though it shares its first 20 iterations with production. The cross-seed leg did not test independent draws.

The paper's other point, that cheap centrality gets within a few percent of IMM, suggests a cheap ablation the system lacks: run a PageRank, degree or Katz-Bonacich seed baseline through the same CRN cascade. It would be an ablation only, because stance gating and seed activation are things centrality cannot see. The joint optimizer is untouched by this paper. It is deterministic (no MC), so the CELF++ failure mode cannot occur there.

Its CV rose to 71.5 percent at 500 nodes. The authors attribute the gap to MC budget and Python implementation but do not test that. The abstract gives 11.2 percent, which conflicts with the body.

paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this paper. His joint-optimizer position treats adaptive greedy plus CELF as the operational layer, with GCOMB-style learned policies taking over at scale. The paper does not threaten that position for optimize.py, which is deterministic. For MC-driven greedy (frontier, coalition), the paper supports it only when marginal estimates are reliable. At 533 nodes, scale is not the binding constraint, so the paper gives no reason to move to RIS, IMM or a learned policy; the brain note 'RIS/IMM unneeded at 533 nodes' agrees. On centrality, Paul says more research on forms of centrality is needed, and the paper adds that PageRank and betweenness are equivalent as spread proxies. That evidence comes only from undirected graphs with uniform p, so it does not touch his interest in directionality (Haythornthwaite) or the retirement of direction-blind centrality. The system-side record is what is stale: the cross-seed MC stability claim predates the 2026-10-01 SEED-keying fix.
